entities.name: Assyrian Evangelical Church
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Assyrian Evangelical Church (also known as the Evangelical Church of the East among Assyrian communities) is one of the Protestant denominations that emerged among Assyrian Christians (also known as Nestorian Christians, or members of the Assyrian Church of the East) through the work of American Presbyterian and later British missions in the 19th century — representing one of the most significant episodes of Protestant missionary activity in the ancient Christian communities of Mesopotamia and Persia.

Assyrian Christians are among the world's oldest Christian communities: the Assyrian Church of the East traces its origins to the apostolic mission of Thomas the Apostle in Mesopotamia and claims direct succession to the ancient church that spread Christianity eastward along the Silk Road to China and India by the 7th century CE. This ancient church was nearly destroyed by Tamerlane's massacres (1380s-1400s) and subsequently survived as a small minority in the Hakkari mountains of southeastern Turkey and northwestern Persia.

American Presbyterian missionaries arriving in Urmia (Persia, now Iran) in the 1830s found the Assyrian Church of the East in weakened condition and began educational and spiritual work that led to conversions to Protestantism, creating the Assyrian Evangelical Church as a new denomination within the broader Assyrian community. The Assyrian Christians' 20th century experiences — including the Seyfo (Genocide) during WWI, mass displacement, diaspora — gave the evangelical community's survival particular poignancy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Assyrian Evangelical Church — formed through American Presbyterian missions to one of the world's oldest Christian communities, surviving the WWI Seyfo Genocide — is historically significant as a monument to Protestant missionary transformation of ancient Eastern Christianity and Assyrian Christian survival.
